documents.title: Mission and Theory of Change
documents.content:
# Prairie Roots Food Alliance — Mission and Theory of Change

Prairie Roots Food Alliance, Inc. is a 501(c)(3) public charity incorporated in Nebraska in 2016 and based in Grand Island, Nebraska. Programmes run in Hall, Merrick, Howard, Hamilton and Buffalo counties.

## Mission
Prairie Roots Food Alliance makes sure families in rural central Nebraska have reliable access to healthy food, and helps new farmers, including immigrant families, grow that food close to home.

## Theory of change
If rural families can get fresh food in their own towns, schools buy from nearby growers, and beginning farmers get land, training and buyers, then fewer households will go hungry and more food dollars will stay in local farm economies. Building both sides of the local food system at once makes food access and farm livelihoods stronger together.

## Why this region
Many small towns in our five counties have no full-service grocery store, and the nearest one can be a 30-mile drive. At the same time, Grand Island's meatpacking plants have drawn families from Guatemala, Mexico, Somalia and South Sudan, many of whom farmed before they arrived.

documents.title: Programme Descriptions
documents.content:
# Programme Descriptions

## Mobile Pantry
A box truck and volunteer crews hold monthly food distribution stops in 14 rural towns. In 2025-26 we served 1,420 households (3,900 people) and distributed 486,000 pounds of food. A borrowed refrigerated trailer is available for only 5 of the 14 monthly stops, so fresh produce, dairy and meat make up just 35% of what we distribute.

## Farm to School Partnership
We buy produce each week during the school year from 23 local growers and deliver it to 11 rural school districts, reaching about 5,600 students. Growers were paid $96,000 in 2025-26.

## Roots to Market Farmer Training
A 9-month course for beginning farmers, taught in English, Spanish and Somali, with a quarter-acre incubator plot for each trainee at our 12-acre training farm near Grand Island. Classes meet on Saturdays and weekday evenings to fit meatpacking shift schedules. 48 trainees enrolled in 2025-26.

## Plans
- Buy a 26-foot refrigerated cold-storage truck (quoted at $185,000) so all 14 stops can offer fresh food. Running costs (fuel, maintenance and insurance) are estimated at $16,000 a year.
- Add 2 more towns to the Mobile Pantry route in 2027-28.

documents.title: 2025-26 Impact Report
documents.content:
# 2025-26 Impact Report

## Who we serve
- 3,948 people served directly: 3,900 people in 1,420 Mobile Pantry households and 48 Roots to Market trainees.
- About 5,600 students in 11 school districts ate Farm to School produce.
- 68% of pantry households earn below 185% of the federal poverty level; 41% include children under 18; 17% include an adult aged 65 or older.
- 65% of trainees (31 of 48) are members of immigrant or refugee families.

## Outcomes
- 486,000 pounds of food distributed at 14 town stops.
- 91% of surveyed pantry households said they skipped fewer meals.
- $96,000 paid to 23 local growers through Farm to School.
- 41 of 48 trainees (85%) completed Roots to Market; 19 graduates sold produce commercially and 7 became Farm to School suppliers.

## In their words
"I worked nights at the plant and grew peppers on Saturdays. This year the school in Wood River bought my whole harvest." — Roots to Market graduate, 2026

## How we measure
Pounds are logged at every stop. Households are surveyed twice a year, and graduates are tracked for two years.

documents.title: FY2026 Budget Summary
documents.content:
# FY2026 Budget Summary

Annual operating budget (FY2026, year ending June 30, 2026): $680,000.

## Expenses
- Mobile Pantry (food purchasing, fuel, drivers, volunteer coordination): $255,000
- Farm to School Partnership (produce purchases, delivery, coordinator): $142,000
- Roots to Market Farmer Training (instructors, interpreters, training farm): $118,000
- Administration and finance: $98,000
- Fundraising: $67,000

Total expenses: $680,000.

## Revenue mix
- Foundations: 46% ($312,800)
- Individual donors: 20% ($136,000)
- Government (USDA beginning-farmer subaward through Central Plains Agricultural College): 14% ($95,200)
- Corporate and agribusiness gifts: 12% ($81,600)
- Events: 8% ($54,400)

Total revenue: $680,000.

## Notes
- Programme spending is 76% of the budget ($515,000).
- The planned $185,000 refrigerated truck is a separate capital project and is not included in the operating budget. Its running costs of about $16,000 a year will be added to the Mobile Pantry line once it is purchased.

documents.title: Governance and Capacity
documents.content:
# Governance and Capacity

- Board of 9 directors; meets every other month. The board includes two working farmers, a former school nutrition director and a Grand Island community health nurse.
- Most recent audit: FY2025 independent audit completed, clean opinion.
- Staff: 7 full-time, 4 part-time, plus about 210 active volunteers, mostly at Mobile Pantry stops.
- Federal experience: subrecipient of a USDA beginning-farmer award through Central Plains Agricultural College since 2023; we have not yet managed a federal grant directly.
- Grants capacity: one full-time development and grants manager; the executive director spends about 20% of her time on grants.
- Policies in place: food safety and handling policy, volunteer safety policy, language access policy, conflict of interest policy, whistleblower policy.

## Key leaders
- Marisol Ortega-Lind, Executive Director — leads the organisation and funder relationships.
- Dale Hinrichs, Programmes Director — manages the Mobile Pantry, Farm to School and the training farm.
- Amina Warsame, Development and Grants Manager — leads proposals, reporting and the grants calendar.

documents.title: Organisation Overview
documents.content:
# Organisation Overview (approved language)

Prairie Roots Food Alliance helps families across five rural counties of central Nebraska put healthy food on the table, and helps new farmers grow it close to home. Since 2016, our Mobile Pantry has brought food to small towns that have no grocery store; in 2025-26 we served 1,420 households at 14 town stops. Our Farm to School Partnership paid $96,000 to 23 local growers for produce served in 11 rural school districts. Through Roots to Market, beginning farmers, many from immigrant families who work in the region's meatpacking plants, learn to grow and sell their own crops.

opportunities.raw_text:
Great Plains Harvest Foundation — Rural Food Access Grants (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Foundation invites proposals from 501(c)(3) organisations in Nebraska, Kansas and South Dakota that help families in towns of fewer than 10,000 residents get healthy, affordable food. Awards range from $25,000 to $75,000 for one year and may be used for general operating support. Priority goes to groups that bring fresh food to towns without a grocery store, that buy from local producers, and that are led by or closely connected to the communities they serve. Capital purchases and endowments are not eligible. Applicants must submit a current operating budget, their most recent audit or financial review, and a board list. Applications are due by 5 p.m. Central time on the deadline date; late submissions will not be reviewed. No match is required.

questions.prompt: Describe your organisation and the community you serve.
questions.answer: Prairie Roots is the leading food security provider in Nebraska and has been fighting hunger for more than 15 years. We serve over 5,000 people every year in 20 rural towns, which is truly amazing for a small organisation. Our programmes are very impactful and make a big difference in the community. We also help farmers and schools in lots of ways. We are passionate, dedicated and committed to our neighbours, and we believe that everyone deserves food.

Nebraska Farm to Table Trust — Local Food Systems Grants (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Trust funds Nebraska nonprofits and tribal organisations that build markets for local growers by connecting them with schools, food banks, hospitals and other institutional buyers. Grants of $20,000 to $60,000 per year are available for up to two years for programme costs. We especially welcome projects that open doors for beginning farmers and farmers from communities historically left out of agricultural markets. Land purchases and lobbying are not eligible. Applicants must provide a programme budget, a two-page logic model and a letter of support from at least one buyer or grower partner. Full applications are due on the deadline date at 11:59 p.m. Central. Grantees report annually, including dollars paid to local growers.

questions.prompt: Describe the programme you are requesting support for.
questions.answer: We are requesting support for our Farm to School Partnership. Each week during the school year we buy produce from 23 local growers and deliver it to 11 rural school districts in central Nebraska, reaching about 5,600 students. In 2025-26 growers were paid $96,000. The partnership is linked to our Roots to Market Farmer Training: 7 graduates became Farm to School suppliers last year, giving beginning farmers, many from immigrant families, a steady first buyer. One graduate told us, "I worked nights at the plant and grew peppers on Saturdays. This year the school in Wood River bought my whole harvest." The programme's FY2026 budget is $142,000, covering produce purchases, delivery and a coordinator.

questions.prompt: What outcomes do you expect over the grant period, and how will you track them?
questions.answer: Over the grant period we expect to keep buying from at least the 23 local growers who supply us today and to continue serving the 11 school districts and about 5,600 students we reached in 2025-26. We also expect more Roots to Market graduates to join the supplier list, building on the 7 who became Farm to School suppliers this year. We will track dollars paid to growers, the number of growers and districts, and graduate sales, and we follow each graduate for two years after the course.

Prairie Agriculture Futures Fund — New Farmer Enterprise Grants (FICTIONAL SAMPLE)
The Fund supports nonprofits in Nebraska and Iowa that help early-career farmers build profitable, lasting businesses. Grants of $50,000 to $100,000 are awarded over two years. This programme is designed for farmers with 3 to 10 years of experience who are ready to scale up: expanding acreage, adding wholesale buyers, or getting their first operating loan. Programmes that mainly serve people who are new to farming may apply only if they can show a clear path for graduates into this stage. Applicants must provide a 1:1 cash match, documented with commitment letters at the time of application. Funds may not be used for food distribution, and indirect costs are capped at 15%. Grantees report twice a year on participant sales, acreage and access to credit. Applications are due by 5 p.m. Central on the deadline date. We give preference to programmes serving farmers of colour and immigrant farmers.

program_report.title: Programme Progress Report: July 1 – September 30, 2026
program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: July 1 – September 30, 2026

**Grant:** Loup Valley Health Foundation, Healthy Rural Households — $60,000 for the Mobile Pantry (July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027)

## Delivered so far
- 42 distribution stops held: one stop a month in each of our 14 rural towns across Hall, Merrick, Howard, Hamilton and Buffalo counties.
- 121,500 pounds of food distributed.
- 1,160 unduplicated households (3,180 people) served.
- 168 volunteers gave about 2,950 hours at pantry stops.

## Outcomes to date
- In our September household survey, 89% of the 312 households who responded said they skipped fewer meals.
- Fresh produce, dairy and meat made up 35% of food distributed. The borrowed refrigerated trailer was available for only 5 of the 14 monthly stops, which remains our main limit on fresh food.

## In their words
"Before the truck came to our town, fresh milk meant a 30-mile drive. Now my grandkids have it every month." — Mobile Pantry neighbour, Howard County, 2026

## Spending to date
$19,400 of the $60,000 grant has been spent: food purchasing $11,800, drivers $4,500 and fuel $3,100. Spending is on track for the 12-month grant period.

program_report.title: Programme Progress Report: July 1 – October 15, 2026
program_report.content:
# Programme Progress Report: July 1 – October 15, 2026

**Grant:** Elkhorn Valley Agricultural Trust, Beginning Farmer Pathways — $45,000 for Roots to Market Farmer Training (July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027)

## Delivered so far
- The 2026-27 Roots to Market cohort began in September 2026 with 46 beginning farmers enrolled.
- 12 class sessions held, on Saturdays and weekday evenings to fit meatpacking shift schedules, taught in English, Spanish and Somali.
- 2 field days at our 12-acre training farm near Grand Island, where each trainee has been assigned a quarter-acre incubator plot for the spring season.

## Participants and outcomes to date
- 30 of 46 trainees (65%) are members of immigrant or refugee families.
- 44 of 46 trainees (96%) are still enrolled after six weeks.
- The 7 Roots to Market graduates who became Farm to School suppliers in 2025-26 are all supplying again this school year, and our training team continues two-year follow-up with the 41 graduates of the 2025-26 course.

## In their words
"The evening classes in Somali mean I can learn after my shift and still be home for my children." — Roots to Market trainee, 2026

## Spending to date
$16,300 of the $45,000 grant has been spent: instructors $9,200, interpreters $4,100 and training farm costs $3,000.
